add_brands.says: Handprint (Bruce MacEvoy, independent watercolour brand reviews with 2004 lightfastness retests) reviews Robert Doak's line of 27 genuine liquid watercolours made in Brooklyn
Independent artist review: Polish watercolour maker, 140 colours (117 single-pigment), honey-based; 'great paints', became one of reviewer's favourite brands
Britain's only remaining traditional oak-bark tannery, Colyton, Devon, family-run since 1862 on a site tanning since Roman times; leather favoured by shoemakers and craftsmen (maker's own page)

Weaver Leather Supply (seller) names Hermann Oak among 'industry leading tanneries' for veg-tan tooling leather; own site: St. Louis tannery since 1881, five generations (no independent quality page found)
Ohio leathercraft supplier (own page) stocking Hermann Oak and Chahinleather hides, Master Tool machines, Fiebing's dye; existence only

Sheridan County tourism: Sheridan-style leather carving tradition upheld by Barry and Ryan King (Don King's grandsons); Barry King's work shown with Japanese masters. barrykingtools.com: stainless stamping tools for Sheridan-style carving, Sheridan WY
Al Stohlman's books 'Figure Carving' and 'How to Carve Leather' for Craftool Co. were instrumental in introducing leathercraft worldwide (Craftool is now a Tandy tool line)
University of Alabama: amate bark-paper workshop of the Santos Rojas family in San Pablito, Puebla, among Mexican workshops revitalising paper traditions
Xinhua: Otomí amate maker Fausto Santos of San Pablito, Pahuatlán, sells amate sheets and works in his family gallery

Wikipedia: Kyoto maker and seller of natural nihonga pigments (iwa-enogu, gofun) founded 1751, 260+ years; only natural-pigment store left in its area. Kyoto Univ. of Arts (uryu-tsushin) calls it Japan's oldest maker of shinsai iwa-enogu, which only it still makes

add_brands.n: Nakagawa Gofun Enogu (ナカガワ胡粉絵具)
add_brands.says: Maker's own site: Japanese nihonga paints, iwa-enogu mineral pigments, nikawa glue, sumi, tools and gold leaf; existence only

ThePrint: Camlin/Camel, Indian ink maker from the 1930s that popularised art education in Indian schools; Camel art colours, oil pastels, poster colours and the Camel art competition are quintessential for generations of Indian students
Wikipedia: Indian adhesive brand by Pidilite, introduced 1959 as alternative to animal glue; Fevicol MR variant for home, office, arts and crafts; sold across Asia, Africa and Americas
Maker's page: British crewel and tapestry wool since 1835, 430 colours; wool used in Bayeux Tapestry restoration and every stitch of the Great Tapestry of Scotland and the Prestonpans Tapestry
Maker's page: needle and pin maker in Normandy since 1833, gold medal at the 1889 Paris Universal Exhibition, still making needles on historic machines at Saint-Sulpice-sur-Risle
Maker's page: Japanese embroidery floss since 1950 (roots 1924), 500 colours, Kyoto; also sashiko thread; self-described renown only
Coate family growing willow on the Somerset Levels since 1819; visitor centre and willow museum 'from withy bed to basket' (own site)
Westonzoyland, Somerset Levels: grows willow and sells basketry willow, rattan, chair cane, cane webbing, tools and kits (own site)

Handwoven magazine (May 1981) profile: most handloom makers have brief histories, an exception is Nilus Leclerc of Quebec, founded 1876, a century in the same family; Leclerc history (leclerclooms.com) calls it a leading producer of handlooms for over a century

Swedish loom maker: Glimåkra loom factory founded 1950 in Skåne, 12,000 looms in 1980, sold across almost the whole world; GAV (1926) continues Dalarna's 18th-century reed-making tradition (maker's page; Handwoven 1981 ad 'Most Swedish weavers select a Glimåkra loom')
Weaver's blog (InWeave): Finnish loom maker founded 1898, family-owned for 5 generations in Toijala, looms sold worldwide; the author learned to weave on Toika countermarch looms
Maker's page: Polish family wood-turners since 1918, spinning wheels from the 1960s and Harp rigid-heddle loom, exported to Europe, North America and Japan
Maker's page: German kiln maker founded 1947 by Conrad Naber for pottery kilns, Lilienthal/Bremen; self-described quality only
Maker's page: Kingston NY potter-founded maker of slab rollers, wheels, extruders and kilns since 1974; says Potter Studio Magazine panel rated its slab roller best (not independently fetched)
Basecoat Lab independent 7-brand comparison: Army Painter (306 paints) built around speed, Speedpaint line; Spikey Bits test names it best budget/easiest
Basecoat Lab: Pro Acryl, pigment-heavy smooth-flowing opaque coverage; with Vallejo has reputation for best quality control/consistent flow
Spikey Bits (hobby site testing paints itself, judged on coverage, flow, finish): Scale 75 best for realism / ultra-matte finish; Basecoat Lab: fine-art style pigments for showcase painting
Spikey Bits paint test: Two Thin Coats best for blending
Spikey Bits paint test: Turbodork best for wild (colour-shift) effects, sold in most gaming stores
FineScale Modeler forum: Testors is probably the most popular model paint, making acrylic, enamel and lacquer lines (US hobby-shop icon)
IPMS/USA review: Mission Models acrylic airbrush paints very forgiving, durable, a different kind of model paint

Norwegian yarn mill since 1888, largest hand-knitting yarn producer in Northern Europe (15 million balls a year); holds the Marius sweater, 'one of the most knitted garments in Norwegian history'; Peer Gynt yarn since 1938 (stockist blog plus maker's about page)
Finnish family spinner since 1928, largest handicraft-yarn maker in the Nordics; its 7 Veljestä sock yarn (1970s) is 'Finland's most loved and iconic yarn' (maker's page)
Danish yarn and pattern house since 1977 continuing designer Åse Lund Jensen's 1960 studio rooted in Danish knitting tradition (maker's page)
Italy Segreta: Amalfi's last handmade paper mill, Amatruda family making rag (bambagina) paper by hand for 700+ years in the Valle dei Mulini; own site: conforms to UNI 10332 maximum permanence
Bassano del Grappa decorated-paper printer since 1957, continuing the Remondini printing house's woodblock decorative papers with the Museo Civico; origami and craft papers (maker's page)
